Every litre of jet fuel at this airport arrives already certified. So why does the fuel farm spend hours refusing to use it?
Here's the farm. Fuel arrives by pipeline, rests in big storage tanks, then flows out through filters to the aircraft. In, rest, out.
But overnight, the air cools. The tanks breathe in damp air, and water dissolved in the fuel comes out as tiny droplets.

Water is heavier than fuel, so it sinks. JIG design is built on that. Tank floors slope down to a drain called a sump. New fuel must settle before it moves. And a floating suction draws only from near the top.
So the waiting isn't slowness. It's gravity doing the cleaning. Every day, sumps are drained, and a sample jar must look clear and bright, with no free water.
Skip a step, and water rides along. At cruising altitude it can freeze into ice crystals that clog an aircraft's fuel filters.
A final filter water separator strips the last drops, and every release is signed and recorded. Gravity, time, and testing. That is how a fuel farm keeps water out of the wing.
